explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. At Patara they find a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, so they board it and set sail (Acts 21:2). Notice the crew doesn't wait around for a perfect plan. They spot a ship going their direction and hop on.

Macedonia is a fair guess, since Paul's crew has traveled around that part of the world. But the text says the ship at Patara is crossing over to Phoenicia (Acts 21:2). Macedonia isn't on this ticket.
Galatia sounds like a place Paul would go, I'll give you that. But this ship is crossing over to Phoenicia, and the crew boards it and sets sail (Acts 21:2). Galatia never comes up in these verses.
That's it, baker. The ship was to unload its cargo at Tyre (Acts 21:3). The ship had business to do, and Paul's crew simply landed along with it. Plain old delivery day.
Soldiers would make this a very different trip. The text says the ship was to unload its cargo at Tyre (Acts 21:3). Nobody in these verses is marching off that boat.
Horses on a boat? I'd pay to see that, but the text doesn't show it. The ship was at Tyre to unload its cargo (Acts 21:3). That's all it tells us about what was on board.

explanations.answer: Not to go up at all
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem (Acts 21:4). Notice the word "kept." This wasn't a one-time comment over dinner.
This one is the opposite of what the text says. Through the Spirit the disciples kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem (Acts 21:4). They were pushing the brakes, not the gas.

Nice thought, but the text never says they asked to come along. It says that through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem (Acts 21:4). Their message was about Paul's trip itself.

Not quite, baker. After the warnings, the text says that when their time there had ended, Paul's crew set out on their journey (Acts 21:5). Paul didn't call off anything. He kept heading toward Jerusalem.

Correct. When their time in Tyre had ended, they set out on their journey (Acts 21:5). The warnings were real, and Paul kept going anyway. He had already told the Ephesian elders the Spirit was warning him in town after town (Acts 20:23).
You got it, baker. The disciples, with their wives and children, knelt down on the beach to pray with Paul's crew (Acts 21:5). That's a whole church on its knees in the sand. No fancy stage needed.
A hymn on the beach sounds lovely, but the text doesn't mention one. It says they knelt down on the beach to pray with Paul's crew (Acts 21:5). The goodbye was a prayer.

explanations.answer: Read a letter from Ephesus together
explanations.explanation: There's no letter in this scene, friend. The text says the disciples knelt down on the beach to pray with them (Acts 21:5). Ephesus was a place Paul had already left behind.

That's right, baker. After the farewells, Paul's crew went aboard the ship, and the disciples returned home (Acts 21:6). Goodbyes on the beach, then two different directions. I think it was a quiet walk back for them.
Not this time. The text says that after the farewells, the crew went aboard the ship, and the disciples returned home (Acts 21:6). They didn't sail along. Their trip ended on that beach.

Yes, baker. Agabus, a prophet from Judea, took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and spoke about the owner of that belt (Acts 21:11). He didn't leave any doubt about who the message was for. That's a message you can see before you even hear it.
Philip, the evangelist whose home they were staying in, is a good guess since the scene is at his house. But the text says Agabus took Paul's belt (Acts 21:11). Philip's belt stayed on Philip.

That one makes sense if you picture someone tying himself up. But the text says Agabus took Paul's belt, then bound his own feet and hands with it (Acts 21:11). He borrowed it from the man the message was about.

That's the one, baker. Agabus says, "…the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles." (Acts 21:11) Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. Heavy words, so I think everyone in that room went quiet.

Samaritans are a real group in the Bible, but they aren't in this prophecy. Agabus says the Jews of Jerusalem will "…hand him over to the Gentiles." (Acts 21:11) Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish.

The Philistines were old enemies of Israel in earlier Bible times, so I see why they came to mind. But Agabus says the belt's owner will be handed over "…to the Gentiles." (Acts 21:11) That's the group named in the prophecy.
Correct, baker. Paul answers, "Why are you weeping and breaking my heart?" (Acts 21:13) His friends were pleading out of love, and I think it really did hit him in the heart. That's a tender moment.
This one is true, friend. Paul really does ask them, "Why are you weeping and breaking my heart?" (Acts 21:13) The people pleading with him were weeping, and Paul said so out loud.

explanations.answer: To be bound and even to die
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." (Acts 21:13) That's a man who has made up his mind, and he says exactly what he's ready for and who it's for.

explanations.answer: To argue his case in court
explanations.explanation: A court case isn't what Paul talks about here. He says, "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." (Acts 21:13) He names being bound and dying.

explanations.answer: To preach and then slip away
explanations.explanation: Slipping away isn't in Paul's answer at all. He says, "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." (Acts 21:13) No escape plan, friend. Just readiness.

Not quite, baker. The text says that when Paul would not be dissuaded, his friends quieted down and said, "The Lord's will be done." (Acts 21:14) The pleading stopped. They went from begging to saying that sentence.

Right. When Paul would not be dissuaded, his friends quieted down and said, "The Lord's will be done." (Acts 21:14) The pleading stopped. I think that was a hard thing to say, and they said it anyway.
That's right, baker. Some of the disciples from Caesarea accompanied them to Jerusalem (Acts 21:16). They'd just heard Agabus and joined the trip anyway. That's a good friend's kind of company.

The Tyre disciples said their goodbyes on the beach, and they returned home (Acts 21:6). The ones who go along to Jerusalem are some of the disciples from Caesarea (Acts 21:16). Tyre was already way back down the coast.

The Ephesian elders, the church leaders Paul had spoken to before, are back in Ephesus. They aren't part of this stretch of the trip. The text says some of the disciples from Caesarea accompanied Paul's crew (Acts 21:16).
